title:
The Emperor deposed, the Prince of Chenliu takes the throne
Plotting against Dong Zhuo, Cao Cao presents a blade
paragraphs:
Now [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) would have killed [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), but [Li Ru](char-li-ru) stopped him. "Things remain unsettled. There must be no rash killing." Yuan Shao bade the officials farewell and went out with the sword still in his hand, hung up his staff of office at the east gate, and rode away to [Ji Province](loc-ji-province). Dong Zhuo said to [Yuan Wei](char-yuan-wei), the Grand Tutor: "Your nephew was insolent, but for your sake I pass it over. And what do you say to the change of emperors?" "You see it rightly, Grand Commandant," said Yuan Wei. "Whoever dares stand in the way of the great design answers for it under martial law," said Dong Zhuo. The ministers were cowed, and answered with one voice: "In everything we obey you." When the feast broke up, Dong Zhuo asked Zhou Bi the Palace Attendant and Wu Qiong the Colonel: "What will come of Yuan Shao's going?" "He went off in a rage," said Zhou Bi, "and if you press the hunt for him he will make trouble for certain. Four generations of the Yuans have sown favors, and their pupils and their old subordinates are spread over the whole realm. If he gathers the bold spirits and draws a following, the heroes will rise at his back, and the lands east of the mountains will be yours no longer. Better pardon him and make him Grand Administrator of some commandery. He will be glad to have his offense forgiven, and there will be no trouble." "Yuan Shao loves plans yet lacks decision," said Wu Qiong. "There is nothing to fear from him. Far better give him a commandery, and win the people's hearts by it."
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) took their advice, and that same day sent to appoint [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) Grand Administrator of [Bohai](loc-bohai). On the first of the ninth month he bade the [Emperor](char-prince-bian) ascend the Jiade Hall, and gathered the whole body of the officers, civil and military. Dong Zhuo drew his sword and held it in his hand. "The Son of Heaven is dull and weak, and not fit to be lord of the realm," he said to the company. "Here is the writ of it, which shall now be read out." And he had [Li Ru](char-li-ru) read it: "[Emperor Xiaoling](char-emperor-ling) early forsook his servants and his people. The Emperor succeeded to the line, and all within the seas looked up to him. But the Emperor is light and frivolous by nature, without reverence in his bearing, slack and idle in his mourning. His want of virtue is manifest, and he disgraces the great seat. The [Empress Dowager](char-empress-he)'s teaching has nothing of a mother's example in it, and her rule has been negligent and disordered. The [Yongle Dowager](char-empress-dowager-dong) died of a sudden, and men doubt the cause of it. Broken are the way of [Three Bonds](misc-three-bonds) and the ordering of Heaven and Earth. [Xie](char-prince-xie), Prince of Chenliu, is great in sagely virtue, grave and exact in his conduct; he mourned with true grief, and no crooked word has passed his lips, and his good report and fair fame are known throughout the realm. He is fit to take up the great inheritance and carry the line down through ages to come. The Emperor is therefore put down to be Prince of Hongnong, and the Empress Dowager resigns the government. Let the Prince of Chenliu be raised to be Emperor, in answer to Heaven and in accord with men, to content the hope of all living."
When [Li Ru](char-li-ru) had made an end of reading, [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) barked at those about him to hand the [Emperor](char-prince-bian) down from the throne. They took the seal and its ribbon from him and made him kneel upright with his face to the north, owning himself a subject and waiting on command. The [Empress Dowager](char-empress-he) too was called upon to put off her robes and await the decree. Emperor and Dowager wept aloud together, and every minister present grieved. Then one great officer below the steps cried out: "Traitor Dong Zhuo, dare you lay a plot to cheat Heaven! The blood of my throat shall spatter you!" And he swung the ivory tablet in his hand straight at Dong Zhuo's head. Dong Zhuo in a great rage shouted to his guards to take the man: it was Ding Guan of the Secretariat. Dong Zhuo had him dragged out and beheaded. Ding Guan cursed him without ceasing, his expression unchanged to the moment of death. A later poet sighed:
> The traitor Dong Zhuo nursed his dark design;
> To grass and rubble went the Han's great shrine.
> A court of ministers sat mute as stone.
> Ding Guan was man enough, and he alone.
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) then desired the [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie) to go up into the hall. When the ministers had made their homage and their congratulation, Dong Zhuo had [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he) taken to the Yong'an Palace to live idle there, with the [Prince of Hongnong](char-prince-bian) and the Emperor's consort [Lady Tang](char-lady-tang); the palace gates were sealed and barred, and no officer might enter without leave. Pity the young Emperor, who came to the throne in the fourth month and in the ninth was put down. The Prince of Chenliu whom Dong Zhuo set up was Xie, styled Bohe, second son of [Emperor Ling](char-emperor-ling) — known to later ages as Emperor Xian — and he was nine years old. The reign style was changed to [Chuping](misc-chuping). Dong Zhuo became Chancellor of State. He was announced at court by his office and not his name, walked to his place without hastening his steps, and came up into the hall still armed and shod; for power to make or mar there was no equal. [Li Ru](char-li-ru) urged him to raise men of name to office and so win the regard of the world, and spoke of [Cai Yong](char-cai-yong)'s ability. Dong Zhuo sent to summon him, and Cai Yong would not come. In anger Dong Zhuo sent a man to tell him: "If you do not come, your whole clan will be destroyed." Cai Yong took fright and had no choice but to obey. Dong Zhuo was delighted to see him, advanced him three times in a month, made him a Palace Attendant, and held him dear.
Now the [young Emperor](char-prince-bian) was penned in the Yong'an Palace with [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he) and [Lady Tang](char-lady-tang). Clothing and food grew scantier by degrees, and his tears were never dry. One day he chanced to see a pair of swallows flying in the court, and made a poem:
> The tender grass is green with gathered haze,
> A pair of swallows weave their slender ways.
> The Luo runs by, one thread of living blue;
> The men upon the road call blest the view.
> I gaze far off where azure cloud is rolled;
> There are the palace halls I had of old.
> Where is the man to take the loyal part,
> And vent the bitterness within my heart!
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) had men constantly on the watch, and that day they brought the poem to him. "He makes verses out of his grudge," said Dong Zhuo. "Now there is good ground to kill him." So he ordered [Li Ru](char-li-ru) to take ten armed men into the palace and make an end of the [Emperor](char-prince-bian). The Emperor was in an upper room with the [Empress Dowager](char-empress-he) and [Lady Tang](char-lady-tang) when a palace maid announced Li Ru, and the Emperor was struck with terror. Li Ru offered him a cup of poisoned wine, and the Emperor asked what it meant. "The spring days are soft and warm," said Li Ru, "and Chancellor Dong sends up wine of long life." "If it is wine of long life," said the Empress Dowager, "you may drink first." "You will not drink?" said Li Ru angrily, and called his men to set a short sword and a length of white silk down before them. "If you will not have the wine, take one of these!" Lady Tang knelt and begged him: "Let me drink in the Emperor's stead, and spare the mother and the son their lives." Li Ru barked at her: "And who are you to die for a prince?" Then he lifted the cup to Empress Dowager He. "You shall drink first!" The Dowager fell to railing at [He Jin](char-he-jin) and his want of judgment, that had brought the traitor into the capital and made this day's ruin. Li Ru pressed the Emperor hard. "Let me take my leave of the Empress Dowager," said the Emperor; and he broke into bitter weeping and made a song:
> The earth is changed, the lights of heav'n decline;
> The throne is cast away, a princedom mine.
> A subject presses me, my days must wane;
> The great tide ebbs, and all my tears are vain!
[Lady Tang](char-lady-tang) made a song too:
> Great Heaven falls, and Sovereign Earth gives way;
> I am his lady, yet must live and stay.
> Living and dead on sundered roads we go;
> What shall I do? So early left in woe!
The song done, they clung to one another and wept. [Li Ru](char-li-ru) barked at them: "The Chancellor of State waits for my report! Whose rescue do you expect?" The [Dowager](char-empress-he) burst out cursing: "The traitor Dong Zhuo drives my son and me to this, and August Heaven does not protect us! You that serve his wickedness, your clans shall be destroyed to the last of them!" Li Ru in a great rage caught her up in both hands and flung her headlong down from the tower, shouted to his men to strangle [Lady Tang](char-lady-tang), and poured the poisoned wine down the [young Emperor](char-prince-bian)'s throat till he was dead. Then he went back and reported to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), who had them buried outside the walls. From that time Dong Zhuo went into the palace every night, forced the palace women, and slept in the imperial dragon bed. Once he took his troops out of the city and came to the neighborhood of Yangcheng. It was the second month, and the village people were keeping the festival of the god of the soil, men and women gathered together. Dong Zhuo had his soldiers ring them round and kill the men, every one, and carried off the women and their goods loaded on carts, with above a thousand heads hung beneath, and came back to the capital in one long train, giving out that he returned from a great victory over brigands. Under the city gate he burned the heads, and parcelled out the women and the goods among his soldiers.
Wu Fu, Colonel of Picked Cavalry, styled Deyu, had seen [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s cruelty and burned with indignation. He took to wearing a light coat of mail under his court robes with a short sword hidden in it, and watched for his chance. One day, as Dong Zhuo came to court, Wu Fu met him below the chamber and struck straight at him with the drawn sword. Dong Zhuo was a strong man and caught him by both wrists, and [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) came in at once and hauled Wu Fu down. "Who taught you to rebel?" said Dong Zhuo. Wu Fu glared at him and shouted: "You are not my sovereign and I am not your subject. Rebellion against whom? Your crimes fill heaven, and every man alive would gladly have the killing of you! My one grief is that I cannot tear you apart with chariots and make amends to the realm!" Dong Zhuo in a great rage had him dragged out and cut to pieces, and to the moment of death the curses never left his lips. A later poet praised him:
> Of Han's last loyal men they tell Wu Fu,
> A heart that stormed the sky as none could do.
> He struck at the traitor in open hall;
> A man indeed, and so shall ages call.
From that day [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) went nowhere without a guard of mailed men about him. [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), at [Bohai](loc-bohai) by this time, heard how Dong Zhuo played with power, and sent a man with a secret letter to [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun). The substance of it ran: "The traitor Dong Zhuo cheats Heaven and has put down his sovereign, and his crimes are past speaking of; yet you let him work his will unchecked, as though you heard nothing of it. Is that the part of a servant who repays the state and keeps his loyalty? I am gathering troops and drilling men, meaning to sweep the royal house clean, but I dare not move rashly. If you are of the same mind, watch your chance and lay your plan. If you have any use for me, I am at your command."
[Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) had the letter, and turned it over in his mind, but found no way. One day, in the waiting chamber at court, he saw the older ministers all together. "Today is this old man's birthday," he said. "Will you gentlemen stoop to come to my house this evening and take a cup?" "We shall certainly come and drink your health," they said. That evening Wang Yun set out a feast in the back hall, and the great officers all came. When the wine had gone round several times, Wang Yun of a sudden covered his face and wept aloud. The company asked him in alarm: "Minister, it is your birthday. What is this grief?" "It is no birthday of mine," said Wang Yun. "I wished to speak with you all, and feared [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) would suspect it. Dong Zhuo cheats his sovereign and plays with power, and the altars of the land may fall any morning or evening. Think how [Gaozu](char-emperor-gaozu) cut down Qin and destroyed Chu and had the whole realm for his own. Who would have thought that, handed down to this day, it should be lost in Dong Zhuo's hands? It is for this that I weep." At that they all wept. Then one of the company clapped his hands and laughed aloud. "The whole court, weeping from dark to dawn and from dawn to dark again — can you weep Dong Zhuo to death?" Wang Yun looked, and it was [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao), Colonel of Cavalry. "Your own forefathers ate the grain of Han," said Wang Yun angrily. "Have you no thought of repaying the state, that you sit there laughing?" "I laugh at nothing else," said Cao Cao, "but that among so many of you there is not one plan to kill Dong Zhuo. Little as I am worth, I will strike Dong Zhuo's head off and hang it at the capital gate, and so make the realm amends." Wang Yun rose from his place. "What is your counsel, Mengde?" "These days past I have bent myself to serve Dong Zhuo for no other reason than to watch my chance at him," said Cao Cao. "He trusts me well enough now, and I can come near him. I hear you have the Seven Gems Sword, Minister. Lend it me. I will go into the Chancellor's residence and kill him, and die for it with no regret!" "If Mengde is truly of that mind, it is great good fortune for the realm!" said Wang Yun, and poured him wine with his own hand. Cao Cao spilled a little on the ground and swore his oath, and Wang Yun fetched the blade and gave it to him. Cao Cao hid it about him, drank off his wine, and rose at once to take his leave of the company. The rest sat a while longer, and then they too broke up.
Next day [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) girded on the blade and came to the Chancellor's residence, and asked where the Imperial Chancellor was. "In the small chamber," said the attendants. Cao Cao walked straight in. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) was sitting on the couch, with [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) standing in attendance at his side. "Why so late, Mengde?" said Dong Zhuo. "My horse is a sorry one and goes slowly," said Cao Cao. Dong Zhuo turned to Lü Bu. "I have good horses sent in from Xiliang. Go yourself, Fengxian, and pick one out for Mengde." Lü Bu took the order and went. Cao Cao said within himself: "The traitor deserves to die!" and was on the point of drawing to stab him; but he feared Dong Zhuo's strength, and dared not move rashly. Dong Zhuo, being fat and heavy, could not sit long, and lay back and turned his face to the wall. "Now he is done for!" thought Cao Cao, and whipped the blade out. He was just at the stroke when Dong Zhuo, looking up into the dressing mirror, saw Cao Cao behind him with the blade drawn, and turned sharply round. "What are you doing, Mengde?"
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) had that moment led the horse up outside the chamber. [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) in his fright dropped to his knees with the blade held out. "I have a fine blade here, and would offer it to you, my gracious lord." [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) took it and looked at it, and saw a blade above a chi long, inlaid with seven jewels and ground to a keen edge — a fine blade indeed. He handed it to Lü Bu to keep, and Cao Cao drew off the scabbard and gave him that too. Dong Zhuo brought Cao Cao out of the chamber to look at the horse, and Cao Cao thanked him. "Might I try a turn on him?" Dong Zhuo had him saddled and bridled. Cao Cao led the horse out of the Chancellor's residence, laid on the whip, and was away to the southeast. "It looked to me just now as though Cao Cao meant to stab you," said Lü Bu, "and when you called out and caught him he put it off as a gift of the blade." "I thought the same," said Dong Zhuo.
They were still talking when [Li Ru](char-li-ru) came in, and [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) told him what had passed. "[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) has no wife or children in the capital and lodges alone," said Li Ru. "Send to call him now. If he comes at once with no misgiving, it was a gift of the blade; if he makes excuses and does not come, it was an attempt on your life for certain, and he may be taken and questioned." Dong Zhuo thought well of it and sent four jailers to summon him. They were gone a good while, and came back with this: "Cao Cao never went back to his lodging. He rode out of the east gate at a gallop, and when the gate officer questioned him he said, 'The Imperial Chancellor sends me on urgent business,' and put his horse to it and was gone." "He has a traitor's heart and has run for it," said Li Ru. "There is no doubt of the attempt now." Dong Zhuo raged: "I raised him so high, and he would have my life!" "He must have had fellows in it," said Li Ru. "We shall know when Cao Cao is taken." So Dong Zhuo sent writs out everywhere with a drawing of his face, for the arrest of Cao Cao: a thousand in gold to whoever took him and handed him over, and a marquisate of ten thousand households; and the same guilt for whoever sheltered him.
Now [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao), once clear of the city, rode hard for Qiao Commandery. On the road he came through Zhongmou County, where the guard on the road took him and brought him before the Magistrate. "I am a travelling merchant, Huangfu by surname," said Cao Cao. The Magistrate looked hard at him and sat pondering a good while. "When I was at [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) seeking office I came to know you for Cao Cao. Why hide it? Put him in the lock-up for the present; tomorrow we take him to the capital for the reward." He gave meat and drink to the men of the guard and sent them away.
In the middle of the night the Magistrate had his own men bring [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) out secretly and take him into the back court to be questioned. "I hear the Imperial Chancellor treated you handsomely. Why bring this ruin on yourself?" "How should swallows and sparrows know the mind of the swan?" said Cao Cao. "You have taken me. Take me up and get your reward." The Magistrate sent his people out of hearing. "Do not think so little of me. I am no common officer; it is only that I have not met my master yet." "My forefathers ate the grain of Han for generations," said Cao Cao. "If I had no thought of repaying the state, how should I differ from the beasts? I bent myself to serve [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) only to watch my chance at him and rid the country of a plague. It has failed, and that is Heaven's will!" "And where were you bound, Mengde?" said the Magistrate. "I was for my own village, to put out a forged edict and call the lords of the realm to arms, that together we might destroy Dong Zhuo. That is my wish."
At that the Magistrate loosed his bonds with his own hands, helped him to the upper seat, and bowed twice. "You are indeed a loyal and upright man of the realm!" [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) bowed in turn and asked his name. "Chen is my surname, [Gong](char-chen-gong) my name, Gongtai my style," said the Magistrate. "My old mother and my wife and children are all in Dong Commandery. Your loyalty has moved me, and I will throw up my office and fly with you." Cao Cao was very glad. That night Chen Gong got money together for the road, and the two of them changed their clothes, slung a sword each on his back, and took horse for Cao Cao's own village.
They had been three days on the road, and came to the neighborhood of Chenggao as the light was failing. [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) pointed with his whip into the deep of a wood. "There is a man here named Lü Boshe, my father's sworn brother. Let us go and ask him for news of my people, and a night's lodging. What do you say?" "Nothing better," said [Chen Gong](char-chen-gong). They dismounted at the farm and went in to Lü Boshe. "I hear the court has writs out everywhere and is hunting you hard," said he, "and your father has gone off to Chenliu out of the way of it. How do you come to be here?" Cao Cao told him all that had happened. "But for Magistrate Chen my bones would have been ground to powder by now." Lü Boshe bowed to Chen Gong. "But for Your Lordship, my young nephew's whole house would have been wiped out. Sit at your ease, Your Lordship; you shall have a bed in my poor cottage tonight." With that he rose and went within, and after a good while came out again. "I have no good wine in the house," he said to Chen Gong. "Let me go to the west village and buy a jar to set before you." And he got on his donkey in haste and rode away.
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) and [Chen Gong](char-chen-gong) had sat a good while when they heard the whetting of a knife behind the house. "Lü Boshe is no blood kin of mine," said Cao Cao, "and there was something doubtful in his going. Let us listen." The two stole round behind the thatched hall, and heard a voice say: "Tie them up before we kill them — how will that do?" "There it is!" said Cao Cao. "Strike first, or we shall be taken." So the two drew and went straight in and killed them all, men and women alike, eight of them one after another. Searching on to the kitchen, they found a pig bound there for killing. "You think too much, Mengde," said Chen Gong. "We have killed honest people in error!" They hurried out of the farm, mounted and rode. Not two li on they met Lü Boshe coming with two jars of wine slung at his saddlebow and fruit and greens in his hand, and he called out to them: "Why are you off so soon, nephew, and Your Lordship?" "Men under a charge dare not stay long," said Cao Cao. "I told them at home to kill a pig for your dinner," said Lü Boshe. "Can you not spare one night, nephew, and Your Lordship? Turn your horses, I beg."
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) took no notice and whipped his horse on. He had not gone a few paces when he drew his sword, turned back, and called to Lü Boshe: "Who is that coming there?" Lü Boshe turned his head to look, and Cao Cao swung the sword and cut him down from the donkey. "Last was a mistake," said [Chen Gong](char-chen-gong), appalled. "But what is this?" "Let Lü Boshe get home and find all those dead, and is he likely to let it go?" said Cao Cao. "He will raise the countryside and come after us, and we shall be ruined by it." "To kill him knowing the truth is a great wrong!" said Chen Gong. "Better I wrong the world than the world wrong me," said Cao Cao. Chen Gong said nothing.
That night they rode some li further and knocked up an inn by moonlight and took lodging. When the horses were fed, [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) lay down first and slept. [Chen Gong](char-chen-gong) lay thinking: "I took Cao Cao for a good man and threw up my office to follow him, yet he proves to be a cold-hearted wretch! Leave him alive today and he will be a plague hereafter." And he made to draw his sword and kill Cao Cao. Truly:
> No worthy man bears so malign a mind;
> Cao Cao and Dong Zhuo prove the same in kind.
Whether Cao Cao kept his life, the next chapter will tell.

versions.name: Cai Yong
versions.description: Style name Bojie. A renowned scholar of Han, serving as Court Counselor.

versions.name: Cai Yong
versions.description: Style name Bojie. A renowned scholar of Han, serving as Palace Attendant.

versions.name: Cao Cao
versions.description:
Style name Mengde. Grandson of the eunuch Cao Teng by adoption.
Serves as Colonel.

versions.name: Cao Cao
versions.description:
Style name Mengde. Grandson of the eunuch Cao Teng by adoption.
A fugitive, hunted on [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s command after his attempt to kill him.

versions.name: Chen Gong
versions.description: Style name Gongtai. Serves as Magistrate of Zhongmou County.

versions.name: Chen Gong
versions.description:
Style name Gongtai.
Gave up his magistracy to follow [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao).

versions.name: Ding Yuan
versions.description: Style name Jianyang. Inspector of Jing Province. Killed in his own tent by his foster son [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu).

versions.name: Dong Zhuo
versions.description: General of the Vanguard, Marquis of Aoxiang and Inspector of Xiliang.

versions.name: Dong Zhuo
versions.description: Chancellor of State, and master of the court.

versions.name: Emperor Gaozu
versions.description: Personal name Liu Bang, founding emperor of the Han dynasty; rose from commoner origins to overthrow the Qin and establish the Han.

versions.name: Emperor Ling
versions.description:
The reigning Han emperor at the novel's opening.
Died of illness.

versions.name: Empress Dowager Dong
versions.description:
Mother of [Emperor Ling](char-emperor-ling).
Driven from the palace by [He Jin](char-he-jin) and [Empress He](char-empress-he), then secretly poisoned.

versions.name: Empress Dowager He
versions.description: Sister of the Grand General [He Jin](char-he-jin); mother of [Emperor Shao](char-prince-bian). Of humble origin from a butcher's household.

versions.name: Empress Dowager He
versions.description:
Sister of the Grand General [He Jin](char-he-jin); mother of the [Prince of Hongnong](char-prince-bian). Of humble origin from a butcher's household.
Shut up in the Yong'an Palace by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Empress Dowager He
versions.description:
Sister of the Grand General [He Jin](char-he-jin); mother of the [Prince of Hongnong](char-prince-bian). Of humble origin from a butcher's household.
Thrown from a tower by [Li Ru](char-li-ru).

versions.name: He Jin
versions.description:
Grand General of Han. Born to a butcher's household, and raised to power when his sister became [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he).
Killed inside the palace by [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and the Ten Attendants.

versions.name: Lady Tang
versions.description: Consort of the [Prince of Hongnong](char-prince-bian).

versions.name: Lady Tang
versions.description:
Consort of the [Prince of Hongnong](char-prince-bian).
Strangled by [Li Ru](char-li-ru)'s men.

versions.name: Li Ru
versions.description: Son-in-law and counselor to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Lü Bu
versions.description:
Style name Fengxian. Foster son of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo); killed his former foster father [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan).
Serves as Cavalry Commandant, General of the Household and Marquis of the Capital Village.

versions.name: Emperor Shao
versions.description:
Previously Prince Bian. Elder son of [Emperor Ling](char-emperor-ling); his mother is [Empress He](char-empress-he).
Succeeded his father as Emperor.

versions.name: Prince of Hongnong
versions.description:
Previously Emperor Shao. Elder son of [Emperor Ling](char-emperor-ling); his mother is [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he).
Deposed by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) and shut up in the Yong'an Palace.

versions.name: Prince of Hongnong
versions.description:
Previously Emperor Shao. Elder son of [Emperor Ling](char-emperor-ling); his mother was [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he).
Deposed by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), and poisoned in the Yong'an Palace by [Li Ru](char-li-ru).

versions.name: Prince of Chenliu
versions.description: Previously Prince Xie. Younger son of [Emperor Ling](char-emperor-ling); his mother, Lady Wang, was poisoned by [Empress He](char-empress-he), and he was raised in the palace of his grandmother [Empress Dowager Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong).

versions.name: Emperor Xian
versions.description:
Previously Prince of Chenliu. Style name Bohe. Younger son of [Emperor Ling](char-emperor-ling); his mother, Lady Wang, was poisoned by [Empress He](char-empress-he), and he was raised in the palace of his grandmother [Empress Dowager Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong).
Set on the throne by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) at the age of nine.

versions.name: Emperor Xian
versions.description:
Previously Prince of Chenliu. Style name Bohe.
Set on the throne by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) at the age of nine.

versions.name: Wang Yun
versions.description: Minister of the Masses, one of the [Three Ducal Ministers](misc-three-ducal-ministers).

versions.name: Yuan Shao
versions.description:
Style name Benchu. Of the great Yuan house.
Serves as Colonel of the Central Army.

versions.name: Yuan Shao
versions.description:
Style name Benchu. Of the great Yuan house.
Serves as Grand Administrator of [Bohai](loc-bohai).

versions.name: Yuan Shu
versions.description: Younger brother of [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao); of the great Yuan house.

versions.name: Yuan Wei
versions.description: Grand Tutor, and uncle to [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) and [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu).

versions.name: Zhang Rang
versions.description: Chief of the Ten Attendants. Drowned himself in the river below [Mount Beimang](loc-beimang).

versions.name: Mount Beimang
versions.description: A line of low hills just north of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang), long used as a burial ground.

versions.name: Bohai
versions.description: A commandery of [Ji Province](loc-ji-province).

versions.name: Ji Province
versions.description: A Han province of the northern plain, north of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang).

versions.name: Luoyang
versions.description: Capital of Han at the novel's opening.

versions.name: Chuping
versions.description: A reign-era of [Emperor Xian](char-prince-xie), beginning in 190 CE.

versions.name: Three Bonds
versions.description: The three cardinal relations of Confucian teaching: ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife.

versions.name: Three Ducal Ministers
versions.description: The three highest-ranking civil officials of the Han court: the Grand Commandant, the Minister of the Masses, and the Minister of Works.
